summary: The priest’s garments show the splendor an adornment gives. Yahweh glorifies his sanctuary and his people, and the singer praises his splendor. The same consonants also name boughs and the gathering of olives left on them.

words.summary: Also תִּפְאֶרֶת. It describes both the beauty of something seen and the honor of a person or deed that others praise.

senses.definition: Beauty that gives distinction to a garment, building or person.

evidence.note: Aaron’s sacred garments are made for honor and splendor.
The anklets and other ornaments can be taken away.

senses.definition: Excellence that gives people cause to praise someone.

evidence.note: The singer asks that his mouth be filled with God’s praise and his splendor all day.
The nations hear of the good Yahweh does for Jerusalem.
Passing over an offense brings a person honor.

senses.definition: The person or quality in which one finds distinction.

evidence.note: Fathers are their children’s pride.
Strength is the pride of young men.

parallels.note: The singer’s mouth is filled with praise as he tells of God’s splendor.

senses.definition: To adorn a place or confer distinction on someone.

evidence.note: The trees of Lebanon beautify the sanctuary.
Yahweh honors the humble with salvation.

senses.definition: To make one’s glory known through a work or a servant.

evidence.note: Yahweh shows his glory in redeeming Jacob.

senses.definition: To exalt oneself over another or claim an achievement as one’s own.

evidence.note: Israel might boast that its own hand won the victory.
The axe boasts over the one who wields it.
Moses gives Pharaoh the distinction of naming the time for his prayer.

senses.definition: An ornament bound on the head, worn by priests and bridegrooms.

evidence.note: The linen headdresses go on the priests’ heads.
The bridegroom wears one as the bride puts on her jewels.
The mourners receive a headdress in place of ashes.

words.summary: The vine and tree passages show what a bough is. How the word relates to adornment remains uncertain.

senses.definition: A spreading limb of a vine or tree that grows out, casts shade and can be broken off.

words.summary: Isaiah uses this collective once, where the surrounding forest is felled.

senses.definition: The upper branches lopped from the tree.

evidence.note: Lopping the boughs stands alongside cutting down the tall trees.

words.summary: The single use describes the second pass over an olive tree. The tree noun gives the verb its sense.

senses.definition: To gather olives still hanging after the tree has been beaten.

evidence.note: What remains after the beating is left for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow.

words.gloss: a change in the face under terror
words.summary: Both uses describe faces when terror strikes. The exact appearance and its connection with splendor are uncertain.

senses.definition: Something visible on every face as the people are overcome with fear.

evidence.note: The peoples writhe before the advancing force.
Faces change as hearts melt and knees shake.

cognates.note: An Ebla attestation gives the same object as פְּאֵר, but the consonants occur in a different order.

evidence.locator: armep Akkadian glossary x000002390, ʾapru, attested as ʾaprum

note: The database counts the same 14 tokens under both verb keys. The bough verb is the piel of Deu 24:20 alone. The two bough keys likewise share indexed tokens, but the collective belongs to Isa 10:33. q.cs.ad and w.bi.ai are empty cross-references. Paran (q.ad.af) names a wilderness and a mountain, with no clear derivation or personal bearer. The Peshitta fruit noun פֵּארָא belongs with פְּרִי in parah. Arabic faḫara “boast” (Lane, p. 2349) and farʿ “upper part, branch” (p. 2379) offer close meanings but leave the consonant differences unexplained. Does פָּארוּר denote paleness, darkening or another change of complexion?
